chunks: Said Sheikh Abu Ja'far al-Tusi — student of the one described — in al-Fihrist:

Among the theologians of the Imamiyya. The leadership of the Imamiyya in his time culminated in him. He was preeminent in knowledge and the craft of kalam. He was a faqih of the highest rank in it, of excellent sagacity, precise in intelligence, and quick with answers.
And he said in his Rijal, in the section of those who did not narrate from them, peace be upon them: Eminent, trustworthy.

key_terms.الْكَلَامِ: kalam — Islamic scholastic theology; rational defense and systematization of doctrine
key_terms.ثِقَةٌ: thiqa — trustworthy; the technical rijal term certifying a narrator or scholar as fully reliable
key_terms.رِئَاسَةُ: leadership/headship — the supreme scholarly and communal authority of the Imami school
key_terms.فَقِيهًا: faqih — a master jurist versed in Islamic law (fiqh)

ai.seo_question: What praise did Sheikh al-Tusi give his teacher in al-Fihrist and Rijal?
ai.summary: This passage preserves Sheikh Abu Ja'far al-Tusi's twofold testimony to his teacher in al-Fihrist and Rijal: he is identified as the supreme head of the Imamiyya, foremost in both kalam theology and fiqh, endowed with keen intellect and swiftness of response. The concluding rijal verdict — jalil thiqa (eminent and trustworthy) — is the highest evaluative formula al-Tusi employs for scholars who did not directly receive from the Imams (peace be upon them). The subject is widely identified as Sheikh al-Mufid (d. 413 AH), al-Tusi's own teacher and author of al-Muqni'a, the fiqh work that Tahdhib al-Ahkam was written to elaborate.
